texts: I spent a year complaining about my coworkers' laziness, then my manager showed me a list of my own missed deadlines.
I set out to find the wicked one and found none; then I looked inward, and none was worse than I.
doha about how i went looking for bad people and ended up finding myself
I searched for the wicked
Write a doha about the man who went out to find the evil in the world and came back empty-handed, until he turned his gaze on himself and found the one he had been seeking.
skeleton, my own flaws
Even a skeleton stripped bare hides fewer faults than my heart; why then do I count my neighbour's sins?
Compose a verse about the person who keeps listing others' failings, and on seeing a skeleton at the roadside is struck by how many secret failings of his own he has never once examined.
At my uncle's last rites, standing before the skeleton remains, I suddenly saw how long my own list of mistakes was, and stopped judging my brother.
doha on counting others' flaws when i'm a skeleton of mistakes myself
look at my own flaws
Each finger I point at another leaves three pointing back at me; teach me to count them.
Give me a verse about how easy it is to see the faults of other people and how hard it is to notice our own, and how real growth begins on the day we start with ourselves.
need a doha on judging others when i'm not perfect either
I told my friend off for being late and then realized I was forty minutes late to my own sister's birthday last week.
My neighbour complains about everyone's untidy door, and last night I saw how long his own has gone unpainted and broken.
door, own flaws first
Sweep your own doorstep before you complain about your neighbour's dust; the faults at your threshold are many.
Write a verse about the man who stands at his door judging everyone who passes, never noticing the mess behind him, and how the wise one first cleans his own threshold before criticising any other.
doha about pointing out others' faults at the door when mine are bigger
fault-finder finds himself
short doha about finding my own faults
Compose a doha about the humbling moment when a man who has been criticising the crowd finally sees his own errors clearly, and realises the hardest flaw to see is the one he carries.
After losing my temper at the family gathering I realized I had spent years calling others short-tempered.
I scanned the world for crooked hearts, and the crookedest was the one that searched.
Write a verse about the person who sees every grain of salt in others' lives and counts the stars of their failings, while the great darkness of his own mistakes goes unnoticed.
doha on salt and stars: i see others' flaws like stars but ignore mine
The stars are many, and so are my faults; yet I count only the salt in my neighbour's food.
I complained that my friend's cooking was too salty, and later under the stars I admitted I had never cooked a single meal for him.
salt, stars, own faults
i find fault with everyone, doha on checking myself instead
mend myself first
Every dinner I complain about someone, and last Sunday my daughter gently asked what I thought was wrong with me.
Give me a verse about the habit of finding fault with everybody around me and what happens when I finally look at my own conduct honestly and see how much needs mending in me.
A critic of the whole world, I turned at last to myself and found work enough for a lifetime.
Write a doha about the person who stands on a bridge between criticising others and facing himself, and who finally crosses over to examine his own shortcomings and begins to improve.
Walking across the bridge to work, I rehearse what is wrong with my boss, and today I started rehearsing what is wrong with me.
On the bridge between my neighbour's flaws and mine, I stood a long time before I crossed to my own.
bridge, own faults
doha about crossing the bridge from judging them to judging me
I told everyone my aunt was bitter and sharp, until my cousin showed me the angry messages I had sent that very morning.
bitter gourd, my faults
doha on the bitter gourd i keep blaming others for my own bitterness
I called my neighbour's words bitter as a gourd, but the gourd was growing in my own garden.
Compose a verse about the person who complains that others are bitter like a bitter gourd, when the real bitterness grew in his own heart and spoiled every word he spoke.
Write a doha about the person who is a fine judge of others but a poor judge of himself, and who turns the same sharp eye upon his own faults only when life forces him to pause.
judge yourself first
doha on judging myself before judging others
After criticising my brother's bad habits for years, I quit smoking only when I admitted to myself that I had the same habit.
Thousands of mirrors hang in a man's judging eyes, but none turned inward; sing the day it does.
I always thought of myself as a flawless diamond until a friend gently pointed out how often I interrupt and brag.
Write a verse about how a diamond, however brilliant, has its tiny flaws, and how people who admire themselves must look into their own depths and admit the cracks that lie within.
doha on a diamond with a flaw, like me
diamond, hidden flaw
Every diamond hides a flaw in its depths; I call my neighbour cracked and forget my own.
Compose a doha about the habit of blaming others for everything that goes wrong, and about the moment of clarity when we see that most of those troubles started with our own mistakes.
I blamed my partner for our fights for a year, and then, while writing a letter to him, I saw my own part in every one.
doha on blaming others when I'm at fault
blame yourself, not them
O critic, set down your lantern of blame and turn it upon your own steps; there the dark lies thickest.
I pressed my neighbour's failings in the oil press all day; my own seeds of folly lay untouched.
oil press, my faults
Write a doha about the man who spends his days pressing others' mistakes through the oil press of gossip, extracting every drop of shame, while his own mistakes remain unnoticed and untouched.
doha on grinding others' faults in an oil press and ignoring mine
My uncle runs the oil press in our village and delights in telling everyone who failed, never mentioning that his own business failed first.
Compose a verse about the strange blindness that lets a person see every error in another but none in himself, and the quiet honesty required to look at one's own conduct with the same sharp eyes.
When my roommate left a dish in the sink I scolded him, and then I realised there were six of my own cups in the living room.
why do i spot everyone's mistakes but not mine
blind to my own
The eye sees all the world, but not itself; teach it, Lord, to see where it has been wrong.
Write a doha about the man who sets out to count the sins of the whole village and returns with a longer, more embarrassing list of his own failings, humbled and silent.
doha on how everyone else is a saint compared to me once I look
my own sins, counted
I went to count the sins of the whole village and returned with a longer list from my own heart.
I wrote down every flaw of my sister-in-law, then read the list again with my own name at the top, and tore it up.
Searching for the guilty, I found the one who was searching; sing the silence that followed.
doha on admitting i was the problem
Write a verse about the person who blames every quarrel on someone else until the day he is honest enough to admit that he was the source, and feels both ashamed and strangely free.
I was the problem
After three fights with three different friends, I finally asked if the common factor might be me.
Give me a verse for the person who spends all his energy criticising others, asking him to start the work of correction with the one wrongdoer he knows best, himself, and to be patient.
My mother says everyone should sweep their own side of the street first, and I think she's right about me.
start with yourself
doha: stop pointing fingers, fix myself first
Strike the false judge within; set the honest one on his seat, and begin with your own case.
doha about churning up others' faults, but my own butter is spoiled
The churn turns others' sins to froth while my own butter sours; who will turn me?
churn, my faults
Compose a verse on the person who churns the faults of others all day in his talk, producing only froth, while his own failings sit and spoil in the corner of his heart.
My aunt churns the village gossip every afternoon with a cheerful face, never noticing that her own temper has soured.
doha on milk and spotting a fault in others' milk but not mine
I told my sister-in-law the milk she served was not fresh, and the next morning discovered mine had been left out all night.
milk, own faults
Write a doha about the person who spots a tiny speck in his neighbour's milk and loudly complains, never noticing that his own cup is full of something far worse than a speck.
I found a speck in my neighbour's milk and never saw the dust in my own cup.
doha on praying for others at the temple but should pray for myself
temple, own faults
I went to the temple to ask God to fix my brother, and while there I understood God was asking me to fix myself.
Write a verse about the devotee who goes to the temple to pray against others' wickedness, and who finds in the silence that his own wickedness is the thing most in need of prayer.
I went to the temple to ask forgiveness for my neighbour's sins, and returned having confessed my own.
I kept reporting my colleagues' mistakes to the boss, and the boss finally said the only mistake in the room was my attitude.
Give me a verse about the long search for faults in others that ends close by, in the quiet recognition that the one person you really needed to fix was the one doing the searching.
look at yourself first
doha about being the problem instead of them
Seeking the crooked in the crowd, I found the crooked within; humbled, I laid down my judgement.
Compose a doha on the one who is quick to throw a stone at others for their failings, and who feels the stone return to his own heart when he looks honestly at his own record.
I shouted at a boy who threw a stone through the window, then remembered the window I broke as a child and blamed on someone else.
stone, throw at myself
doha on throwing the first stone but I'm no saint
I flung a stone at the sinner; it landed at my own feet, for I was the sinner.
While standing at the temple, I had planned to complain about my neighbour, and I ended up silently asking for forgiveness.
Write a verse about the pilgrim who arrives at the temple to curse the evildoers, and is stopped short by the realisation that the evil he fears lives inside his own mind and needs the first prayer.
doha about visiting the temple, being the sinner myself
temple, my sins
Within the temple I lit no prayer for the wicked; I lit it for the wicked one in me.
My boss roars at every employee's tiny mistakes like a lion, yet could not pass through the needle's eye of admitting that he is the cause of our delays.
Write a doha about the proud lion who criticises every beast he meets for tiny flaws, and about the needle's eye through which he must pass to see the great fault he never noticed in himself.
The lion roars at the jackal's tail; the needle's eye is small, and so is my honesty with myself.
doha on a lion and a needle, find my own faults
lion, needle, my blind spots
I once told my sister that her words were venom, and then I remembered the salt I rubbed into her wound at the party.
I call the other a snake and dismiss his salt; but whose venom was it that bit my friend?
Write a verse about the man who calls everyone poisonous like a snake while his own words have spread more salt in the wounds of others than anybody else's, and who has never admitted it.
doha on salt and a snake: I see others' venom but not mine
salt, snake, my venom
chakor bird, fire, own faults
doha on a chakor bird and fire, blaming others for my burns
Like a chakor bird gulping fire, I kept blaming my friends for my burnout, but the choices that burned me out were all mine.
Compose a doha about the chakor bird who stares at the glow and swallows fire, then blames the beloved for the hurt, as we all blame others for the pain our own habits have caused.
The chakor swallows fire for its beloved and curses the beloved; so I curse others for the burns I made myself.
date palm, net, my errors
I tried to catch my roommate in a lie, and found in the process that I had lied to him about three smaller things.
Write a verse about the man who casts a wide net to catch the mistakes of others and hauls in his own errors instead, and who then sits under the date palm, humbled and thoughtful.
doha on casting a net for others' mistakes and catching mine
The net I cast for another's faults came back loaded with my own, and the date palm of my pride shook.
Our priest, slow as a tortoise, condemns the village's faults every sermon, but my grandmother says no one has ever heard him admit his own.
Write a doha about the priest who preaches against sin with a voice as slow and heavy as a tortoise, yet who is blind to the sins that sit unspoken in his own heart.
tortoise, priest, own faults
doha on a tortoise priest who judges but forgets himself
The tortoise carries its shell so slowly, the priest his sermon so loudly, and neither has examined what lies inside.
Compose a verse about how much easier it is to criticise the whole world than it is to improve oneself by even a little, and how the courage to start with oneself is the real beginning of change.
O mind, in your haste to fault the world you forgot the one fault you can mend.
doha on fixing myself instead of the world
mend only myself
I vowed to change the world after college, and at thirty-five I'm starting with the habit of checking my own temper first.
doha about dew showing my faults on the grass
dew, honest self-look
Dew on the blade shows each fault clearly in the dawn; may I see mine as clearly as I see my neighbour's.
Walking in the early dew I saw the muddy tracks I had made and thought of all the tracks of my mistakes that I never turn back to see.
Write a verse about the clear dew of early morning that shows every imperfection on the grass, and how we should look just as clearly at our own conduct before we point at anybody else.
My brother mocks me for being slow like a tortoise and I mock him for his lion's temper, and our mother says we should both look at ourselves.
Compose a doha about the lion who laughs at the tortoise's slowness and the tortoise who laughs at the lion's fierce temper, each so busy finding the other's flaw that neither learns his own.
lion, tortoise, own faults
The lion mocks the tortoise's slowness; the tortoise mocks the lion's temper; neither sees his own.
doha on a lion and a tortoise: both judge others but forget themselves
The sandalwood does not blame the snakes that coil around it; it asks what in itself draws them close.
sandalwood doha on seeing my flaws
sandalwood, my own faults
Everyone blamed the quarrel on my neighbour, but I sat with sandalwood incense that evening and quietly saw how I had started it.

Write a verse about sandalwood that is surrounded by snakes yet remains cool, and how the wise person, instead of blaming those around him, looks first at what in himself might be calling the trouble.
At the cremation ground the faults of others vanish into smoke; the ones I carry will burn with me alone.
cremation ground, my faults
doha on thinking of my faults at the cremation ground
Standing at the cremation ground after a friend's passing, I wasn't thinking about his flaws, only about how many of mine I had never mentioned.
Write a doha about the visitor at the cremation ground who thought he was there to mourn another and found himself reviewing his own sins, suddenly aware that they follow no one but himself.
In our market a blind man curses every seller, yet when I stopped to listen, I recognised my own complaining in his voice.
doha on a blind man in a market who blames everybody
Compose a verse about the blind man who stands in the market complaining that everyone cheats him, never admitting that his own blindness to his faults is the first thing that has cheated him.
The blind man in the market curses the shopkeeper's cheating, and does not see the coin he has swindled from himself.
blind man, market, own faults
I wrap my faults in a cloth sheet and show the world a pearl; yet the sheet is thin and I know.
I keep my shortcomings hidden under a cloth sheet of good manners, and a friend with a pearl necklace of honesty called me out last week.
Write a doha about the man who covers his faults with a clean cloth sheet and shows the world his pearl of a reputation, but who knows in the quiet of the night what hides beneath.
cloth sheet, pearl, own faults
doha on a cloth sheet and a pearl, my flaws are hidden
Compose a verse about the mourner who stood beside the bier, smelling sandalwood, and spoke of the dead man's faults, only to feel the smoke of his own sins rise to meet him.
By the bier burn the sandalwood and the speech of faults; I counted his, and found my own in the smoke.
sandalwood, bier, own flaws
sandalwood and bier: i judged the dead and I'm no better
At the bier, while sandalwood burned, I heard relatives list the dead man's mistakes, and I thought of all the mistakes the living have not owned.
Write a doha about the tongue that is quick to point out every failing in others and slow to confess a single one of the speaker's own, and about the day it learns to speak against its owner.
After I snapped at my waiter for a small mistake, I thought about the dozens of small mistakes my own tongue has made this month.
tongue, own faults
doha about my sharp tongue and the faults in me
This tongue lists the faults of everyone and has no word for the one who owns it.
I went to the temple determined to expose the hypocrites, and the first one I caught was myself.
I cast a net across the temple floor to catch the wicked and caught my own reflection, trembling.
doha on a net at the temple that caught only me
Write a verse about the zealous person who sets a trap of rules inside the temple to catch the sinners and is caught in it himself, because the greatest sinner there is the one doing the catching.
net, temple, own faults
cage, my flaws
doha about the cage i keep others in, and my own
Compose a doha about the man who locks everybody else in the cage of his criticism, and eventually finds that the bars he built have shut him in with all his own faults, unable to escape.
I put my sister in a cage of my own opinions for twenty years, and at her wedding I found myself locked in with them.
I built a cage of blame for my neighbours; the key turned, and I was the one inside it.
door, tongue, own faults
doha on standing at the door judging others with my tongue
I stood at the door and judged each guest; my tongue was my own accuser, and the door shut on me.
At the family door I loudly criticised each cousin, and my grandmother quietly asked me when I last examined myself.
Write a verse about the man who stands at the door judging each guest with his tongue, and who finds that he himself was the faultiest visitor, having never been invited to examine himself.
doha: the ocean of others' sins and my own drop
Write a verse about the man who surveys the ocean of the world's wrongdoing and sighs, until he realises that the ocean he fears is mostly the vast, unexamined sea of his own small failures.
I stood by the ocean after a bad week, blaming everyone around me, and the waves made me notice how small my excuses were.
ocean, my own sins
The ocean is vast, but the sins I saw in the world were drops beside the ocean I carried within.
Compose a doha about the man who walks through the market scanning each face for dishonesty and finally admits that the one he trusts least is himself.
I walked through the market of the world looking for wicked men, and by evening I had priced myself among them.
doha on looking for bad people in the market
market, my own faults
In the market I kept guessing who was cheating, and on the walk home I asked who among us was really honest.
doha on crossroads: choosing to examine myself
At a crossroads in my life I decided to stop blaming my past and took the harder path of looking at what I had done.
crossroads, own faults
Write a doha about the wanderer who arrives at a crossroads, one path leading outward to condemn others and the other inward to know himself, and who finally takes the harder path.
At the crossroads one road accuses the world, and the other, steeper, accuses me; I chose the steep one.
Compose a verse about the person who keeps shut the door of his own conscience, ignoring the sharp needle of guilt, and who complains instead that the people outside are cruel and pointed.
I locked my door against a friend's honest criticism, but at night, in bed, the needle of his words went on pricking me.
door, needle, own faults
Behind the door the needle of conscience pricks; I pretend not to feel it, then complain of others' sharpness.
doha on a door and needle: my conscience pricks me
My mother-in-law criticises everything I do, but yesterday I saw I do the same to my own children.
Gentle be the judge of others, harsh the judge of self; so the wise find peace.
Write a verse for the person who cannot stop finding fault with others, reminding him to be gentle toward their errors and strict with his own, and to find peace in that reversal.
I always find fault with people, give me a doha to change that
fault-finder finds himself
I spent years hunting for a perfect partner, a philosopher's stone, grinding through relationships like an oil press, before I saw my flaws.
philosopher's stone, oil press, faults
I sought the philosopher's stone in others, ground them in the oil press of blame, and found the prize in my own flaws.
philosopher's stone, oil press, doha on my faults
Write a doha about the man who searches for the philosopher's stone in other people and presses them through the oil press of judgement, and finds the real prize is honestly recognising his flaws.
When I finally said sorry to my brother for what I had done, I felt a weight lift that I'd carried for ten years.
Compose a verse about the courage of admitting a mistake plainly and without excuse, which is harder than finding fault with others and which brings a calm that blaming never gives.
To know my faults is half the wisdom, to mend them the other half, and to blame another is no wisdom at all.
admit and mend
doha on admitting my mistakes
doha on a tree and cotton, spot others' flaws but not mine
I teased my neighbour for his twisted tree full of cotton fluff, and later realised my own garden of habits looked worse.
Compose a verse about the person who points to a crooked tree in his neighbour's yard and the cotton tangled in its branches, yet who has never noticed the crooked growth in his own character.
I saw the crooked tree and the tangled cotton in my neighbour's yard; my own crooked branch I never saw.
tree, cotton, my faults
Write a doha about the priest who watches the bridge and condemns each stranger who crosses it, never realising that the one who needs forgiving most is the one who stands in judgement.
The priest at the bridge near my street scolds every passer-by, and when I asked about himself he went quiet and walked away.
doha on the bridge and priest, who is the sinner
bridge, priest, my sins
The priest points to the sinner crossing the bridge; the sinner points back, and neither sees himself.
Stone in my hand for the sinner, temple in my mind for the saint; I forgot to ask which one I am.
doha on a stone and temple, check myself first
stone, temple, own faults
Compose a doha about the devotee who enters the temple with a stone to hurl at sinners, and who is brought to his knees when he realises he is the one who most needs forgiveness.
I threw a stone in anger at the temple wall, then sat on its steps and wondered about the real cause of my rage.
